articles.title: US GDP growth revised sharply higher to 4.3% in third quarter on strong consumer spending, AI investment
articles.summary: The US economy grew at a faster-than-expected annualised rate of 4.3% in the July-September quarter of 2026, significantly higher than the earlier
articles.body: The US economy grew at a faster-than-expected annualised rate of 4.3% in the July-September quarter of 2026, significantly higher than the earlier estimate of 3.4%, as stronger consumer spending and business investment supported economic activity.The revised estimate, released by the commerce department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on Wednesday, marked the fastest pace of growth in three years. Economists polled by Reuters had expected the figure to be revised up to 3.5%.The economy had expanded at an annualised rate of 2.2% in the April-June quarter, meaning growth nearly doubled in the third quarter.The upward revision reflected stronger-than-previously estimated consumer spending and investment. The BEA said real GDP was revised up by 0.9 percentage point from its advance estimate, primarily due to upward revisions in these two components.Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the US economy, rose at a revised rate of 4.2%, compared with the earlier estimate of 3.8%.Business investment also remained strong. Spending on equipment increased at an annualised rate of 21.8%, up from the previously estimated 20.9%.According to Reuters, business investment has recorded double-digit growth for three consecutive quarters, although economists have warned that this pace could slow as investors scrutinise valuations of artificial intelligence companies.Domestic demand remains strongThe BEA said the acceleration in economic growth compared with the second quarter primarily reflected stronger investment and an upturn in government spending, partly offset by a decline in exports.Imports also increased during the quarter, according to the BEA data.A key measure of domestic demand, real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which excludes inventories, trade and government spending, rose at an annualised rate of 5.8%.This was the fastest increase since the second quarter of 2021 and higher than the earlier estimate of 4.9%.The upward revision in investment was led primarily by intellectual property products, particularly software, while stronger consumer spending reflected increased expenditure on goods, including pharmaceuticals, computer software and accessories, and petrol and other energy products.Higher-income households were driving much of the consumer spending, supported by gains in stock market wealth before the recent AI-led sell-off.Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring have also helped other households sustain expenditure, although wage growth has at times lagged inflation. Households have also been saving less and drawing on their accumulated savings.Corporate profits rise at slower paceDespite the stronger economic expansion, the increase in corporate profits moderated during the quarter.Profits from current production rose by $206 billion in the July-September period, compared with an increase of $384 billion in the preceding quarter, the BEA said.The income-side measure of economic activity also showed strong growth. Gross domestic income (GDI) increased at an annualised rate of 4.4% in the third quarter, compared with a 2.3% rise in the second quarter.The average of GDP and GDI, which is considered a broader measure of economic activity, also grew at a rate of 4.4%.Inflation remains a concernThe revised GDP figures came alongside fresh inflation data that showed continued price pressures in the US economy.The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% year-on-year in October, matching a three-year high recorded in May.The increase was accompanied by higher energy prices and a rise in non-durable goods inflation. The PCE inflation rate remained well above the Federal Reserve's long-term target of 2%, which it has missed for almost six years.The quarterly PCE price index rose by 2.1%, while core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stood at 2.5%, according to the BEA figures.The Federal Reserve had held interest rates steady at its October meeting after raising them in September. With inflation continuing to run above its target, the possibility of another rate increase at its December meeting remained in focus.The strong growth figures underline the resilience of the US economy despite headwinds, including President Donald Trump's tariff policies and higher energy prices linked to the war on Iran.The AI investment boom has also supported economic activity, while economists have pointed to a widening gap between higher- and lower-income households in their ability to sustain spending.Money habits form by age 7.
